The identity also holds after restricting the perimeter measures to any Borel subset of $X$. Thus contact with $B$ is counted in both constructions, their perimeter-support frontiers agree, and their minimizers correspond with the same minimizing value.

<a id="q4:enc:variation-setup"></a>
#### The family of minimizers and the metric derivative

For a minimizing filled set with frontier $T$, let $V_T$ be its unoriented tangent-plane area measure from Equation <a href="#q:geometry:plane-measure" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:geometry:plane-measure">[q:geometry:plane-measure]</a>. Let $\mathcal T$ be the family of minimizing filled sets, modulo null sets, with their regular frontiers, equipped with local $L^1$ and weak plane-measure convergence.

<a id="stmt-q4-enc-area-derivative"></a>
<div id="q4:enc:area-derivative" class="proposition">

**Proposition 84** (Compact minimizing space and right area derivative). *The space $\mathcal T$ is compact and metrizable. For every smooth symmetric two-tensor $h$, the function <a id="q4:enc:metric-area-functional"></a>$$\label{q4:enc:metric-area-functional}
 a'_T(h)=\frac12\int_T\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{T_xT}h\,dA_g$$ is continuous on it. Let $g_s$, $|s|<s_0$, be a smooth path of smooth metrics on $X$, with $g_0=g$, uniformly comparable to $g$, and with uniformly bounded first and second parameter derivatives relative to $g$. Assume that its coordinate spheres have strictly positive outward mean curvature beyond one common radius. If $a(s)$ is its full smooth-cut infimum and $h=\partial_sg_s|_0$, then <a id="q4:enc:area-derivative-formula"></a>$$\label{q4:enc:area-derivative-formula}
 a'(0+)=\min_{T\in\mathcal T}a'_T(h).$$ The minimum is attained. For $s_j\to0$ and any minimizing frontiers $T_j$ for $g_{s_j}$, a subsequence of the filled sets converges to a member of $\mathcal T$, and its plane-area measures in the fixed metric $g$ converge to the corresponding measure.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-enc-area-derivative"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-enc-area-derivative</summary>

*Proof.* Smoothly extend the path through the fixed boundary in one collar. The common mean-convex tail gives uniform confinement directly by the clipping inequality <a href="#q:geometry:clipping" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q:geometry:clipping">[q:geometry:clipping]</a>: the divergence of the outward unit radial normal is positive for every metric in the path beyond the same radius. This is the common-sphere alternative in Proposition <a href="#q:geometry:envelope" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q:geometry:envelope">9</a>; the scaled first-derivative bounds used in its separate density-estimate alternative are unnecessary here. On the resulting fixed compact region, the smooth path has uniform local bounds. The proposition’s localized polar-measure continuity and uniform Grassmann-bundle Taylor expansion give all the assertions, retaining any mass on $B$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-enc-common-plane"></a>
<div id="q4:enc:common-plane" class="proposition">

**Proposition 85** (A common tangent plane for tied minimizers). *On $\mathcal L=\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal T}(T\setminus B)$, the plane $\Pi_x=T_xT$ is independent of the minimizing frontier through $x$ and is continuous in the relative topology. Consequently $x\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{\Pi_x}K$ is single valued and continuous there for every smooth symmetric two-tensor $K$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-enc-common-plane"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-enc-common-plane</summary>

*Proof.* All free frontiers are smooth in dimension four. Proposition <a href="#q:geometry:sheets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q:geometry:sheets">10</a> gives local agreement at a meeting point and continuity as both the point and the minimizing frontier vary. Its proof uses the small-excess theorem on the whole support, with a smooth-ambient mean-curvature bound after rescaling. This supplies the pointwise plane control beyond the integral convergence in Proposition <a href="#q4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:area-derivative">84</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="q4:var:section"></a>
### Variation at equality and localization of the area term

<a id="q4:var:nonnegative-defect"></a>
Throughout this section, $(\Omega,g,K)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Definition <a href="#q4:def:horizon" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:def:horizon">81</a>, and equality holds in Theorem <a href="#q4:thm:numerical-provider" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:thm:numerical-provider">80</a>. Thus $\Omega$ has one end and its only boundary $S$ is a connected, outermost, outer area-minimizing future MOTS. We use the full enclosing-cut convention of Definition <a href="#q4:def:cuts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:def:cuts">79</a>. Set <a id="q4:var:constants"></a>$$\begin{gathered}
 A=\mathop{\mathrm{Area}}_g(S),\qquad m=\sqrt{E^2-|P|^2},\qquad
 r_0=(A/\omega)^{1/3}=\sqrt{2m},\\
 b^0=E/m,\qquad b^i=-P_i/m,\qquad
 \mathfrak m(a)=\tfrac12(a/\omega)^{2/3},\qquad
 c=6\omega\mathfrak m'(A)=2/r_0.
\end{gathered}
\label{q4:var:constants}$$ The strict future timelikeness needed here is already part of Theorem <a href="#q4:thm:numerical-provider" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:thm:numerical-provider">80</a>. For nearby data with charges $(\widetilde E,\widetilde P)$, define the fixed linear charge functional $$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
   =b^0\widetilde E+\sum_{i=1}^4b^i\widetilde P_i.$$ The reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on the future timelike cone gives <a id="q4:var:supporting-charge"></a>$$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
 \ge \sqrt{\widetilde E^2-|\widetilde P|^2}.
\label{q4:var:supporting-charge}$$ Equality holds at the original data. In particular, whenever the varied data satisfy the numerical theorem, their enclosing infimum $a(\widetilde g)$ satisfies $$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
       -\mathfrak m(a(\widetilde g))\ge0.
\label{q4:var:nonnegative-defect}$$ The varied data need not preserve outermostness or outer area minimization: those assumptions are absent from the numerical theorem.

The right-derivative formula in Proposition <a href="#q4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:area-derivative">84</a> accounts for all minimizing frontiers without choosing a differentiable family. It gives the positive-measure identity of Proposition <a href="#q4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:multiplier">91</a>. Compact normal tests and outermostness then localize its area term to $S$ in Proposition <a href="#q4:var:area-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:area-localization">93</a>, supplying the identity used to construct the causal adjoint field in Theorem <a href="#q4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:causal-field">94</a>.

<a id="pm-h-76"></a>
#### Constraint derivatives and a strict direction

<a id="q4:var:active-set"></a>
On the closed unit ball bundle of $g$, introduce $$\begin{gathered}
 C(x,v)=2(\mu(x)+J_x(v))
       =R_g+\tau^2-|K|_g^2+2J_x(v),\qquad |v|_g\le1,\\
 \mathcal A=\{(x,v):C(x,v)=0\}.
\end{gathered}
\label{q4:var:active-set}$$ DEC is equivalent to $C\ge0$ on this bundle. When the metric varies, we identify its unit ball with the original one by the positive symmetric inverse square root. More precisely, if $g_s(V,W)=g(G_sV,W)$, then $I_s=G_s^{-1/2}$ sends the $g$ unit ball isometrically to the $g_s$ unit ball. For a variation $H=(h,p)=(\dot g_0,\dot K_0)$, all derivatives $C'_H$ below include this identification; in particular, $$\dot I_0v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v.$$

<a id="stmt-q4-var-conformal"></a>
<div id="q4:var:conformal" class="lemma">

<a id="q4:var:conformal-C"></a>
<a id="q4:var:conformal-theta"></a>
**Lemma 86** (Conformal constraint identities). *For a positive smooth function $f$, let $g_f=f^2g$ and $K_f=fK$. Using $f^{-1}v$ in the varied unit ball, one has $$\begin{aligned}
 f^2 C_f(x,f^{-1}v)
   &=C(x,v)+6f^{-1}\bigl[-\Delta_g f+K(\nabla f,v)\bigr],
       \label{q4:var:conformal-C}\\
 f\theta_{+,f}
   &=\theta_++3\partial_\nu\log f.
       \label{q4:var:conformal-theta}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $\nu$ points into the exterior and $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-conformal"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-conformal</summary>

*Proof.* Put $\varphi=\log f$. The scalar-curvature and tensor transformations in dimension four are $$R_{f^2g}=f^{-2}(R_g-6\Delta_g\varphi-6|d\varphi|_g^2),
 \quad \tau_f=f^{-1}\tau,
 \quad |K_f|_{f^2g}^2=f^{-2}|K|_g^2.$$ Since $\Delta\varphi+|d\varphi|^2=f^{-1}\Delta f$, they give $f^2\mu_f=\mu-3f^{-1}\Delta_gf$. For the momentum, set $\pi=K-\tau g$, so $\pi_f=f\pi$. The connection difference is $$\widehat\Gamma^a_{ij}-\Gamma^a_{ij}
 =\delta_i^a\varphi_j+\delta_j^a\varphi_i-g_{ij}\varphi^a.$$ Contracting the covariant derivative of $f\pi$ yields $$fJ_{f,i}=J_i+3\pi_{ij}\varphi^j-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g\pi)\varphi_i
          =J_i+3K_{ij}\varphi^j,$$ because $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g\pi=-3\tau$. In particular every trace-gradient term cancels; no extra asymptotic condition on $\tau$ is used. Evaluating on the identified vector $f^{-1}v$ gives $$f^2J_f(f^{-1}v)=J(v)+3f^{-1}K(\nabla f,v).$$ Adding twice the density and momentum identities proves <a href="#q4:var:conformal-C" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:conformal-C">[q4:var:conformal-C]</a>. Finally $\nu_f=f^{-1}\nu$, $H_{f^2g}=f^{-1}(H_g+3\partial_\nu\log f)$, and $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{TS,f^2g}(fK)=f^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{TS,g}K$. Their sum proves <a href="#q4:var:conformal-theta" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:conformal-theta">[q4:var:conformal-theta]</a> with the same oriented normal. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-var-strict-direction"></a>
<div id="q4:var:strict-direction" class="lemma">

<a id="q4:var:phi-properties"></a>
<a id="q4:var:strict-derivatives"></a>
**Lemma 87** (Strict conformal direction). *Choose $$1<q_0<\min(q,2),\qquad 0<\delta<\min(q_0,1),
 \qquad w=r^{-4-\delta},$$ where the end radius is extended to a positive smooth function on $\Omega$. There is a smooth nonnegative function $\phi$, smooth up to $S$, such that $$\partial_\nu\phi=-1\quad\hbox{on }S,\qquad
 -\Delta_g\phi-|K|_g|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g\ge w,\qquad
 \phi=O_2(r^{-2}),\qquad -\Delta_g\phi/w\longrightarrow1.
\label{q4:var:phi-properties}$$ Its limiting Euclidean sphere gradient flux exists and is finite. For $$Q=(2\phi g,\phi K)$$ one consequently has $$C'_Q\ge6w\quad\hbox{on }\mathcal A,
 \qquad -\theta'_Q=3\quad\hbox{on }S.
\label{q4:var:strict-derivatives}$$ Moreover, uniformly for all $|v|_g\le1$ on the end, $C'_Q/w\longrightarrow6$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-strict-direction"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-strict-direction</summary>

<a id="q4:var:phi-equation"></a>
*Proof.* Choose a smooth majorant $d_0\ge |K|_g$ which on the end is a sufficiently large radial multiple of $r^{-1-q_0}$. It can be chosen with all symbol bounds there. We solve $$-\Delta_g\phi
   =d_0\sqrt{|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g^2+r^{-6}}+w,
 \qquad \partial_\nu\phi=-1\text{ on }S,
 \qquad \phi\longrightarrow0\text{ at infinity}.
\label{q4:var:phi-equation}$$

First truncate at a large coordinate sphere $S_R$, imposing $\phi=0$ on $S_R$, and replace $d_0$ in the equation by $t d_0$, $0\le t\le1$. The inner and outer boundary components are disjoint smooth hypersurfaces; there is no corner where the two boundary conditions meet. The $t=0$ problem is the invertible mixed Laplace problem. Every linearization in $\phi$ adds to $-\Delta_g$ a smooth drift of norm at most $d_0$, with homogeneous Neumann data at $S$ and homogeneous Dirichlet data at $S_R$. The maximum and boundary point principles give uniqueness, and the mixed elliptic Fredholm theory then gives invertibility. These are the usual local elliptic and boundary estimates on a fixed smooth truncated domain; see (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001) <a id="pm-cite-77"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)].

Solutions are nonnegative. Indeed a negative minimum cannot occur in the interior because the right side of the equation is positive. At $S$, the outward normal of the truncated domain is $-\nu$, so the prescribed outward derivative is $+1$, also excluding such a minimum by the boundary point principle. The outer Dirichlet value is zero.

For completeness, the continuation bounds do not require a monotonicity assumption in the unknown. Fix $p>4$. The mixed $W^{2,p}$ estimate, the linear growth of the right side in $\,\mathrm d\phi$, and first-derivative interpolation give, on this fixed truncation, $$\|\phi\|_{W^{2,p}}\le C\bigl(1+\|\phi\|_{L^\infty}\bigr),$$ uniformly in $t$. If the supremum were unbounded, division by that supremum and compactness in $C^1$ would produce a nonnegative function $z$ with supremum one satisfying $$-\Delta_g z=t_*d_0|\,\mathrm dz|_g,
 \qquad \partial_\nu z=0\text{ on }S,
 \qquad z=0\text{ on }S_R$$ for some $t_*\in[0,1]$. At points where $\,\mathrm dz\ne0$ the right side is a bounded drift applied to $\,\mathrm dz$, and it is zero otherwise. The strong maximum and boundary point principles for this bounded-drift equation contradict the positive maximum. The resulting $W^{2,p}$ and Schauder bounds close the continuation argument and give a smooth solution at $t=1$ on every sufficiently large truncation.

<a id="q4:var:tail-barrier"></a>
<a id="q4:var:tail-bound"></a>
We next make the bounds independent of $R$. For $W=r^{-2}-r^{-2-\delta}$, the Euclidean identity $$-\Delta_\delta W=(2+\delta)\delta r^{-4-\delta}$$ and the AF estimates imply, beyond a fixed radius $R_1$, $$-\Delta_g W-d_0|\,\mathrm dW|_g\ge c_1w>0.
\label{q4:var:tail-barrier}$$ The metric errors and the drift term are smaller than $w$ because $\delta<q_0<q$. Also $d_0r^{-3}=o(w)$. If $M_R$ is the supremum of the truncated solution on the fixed core bounded by $S_{R_1}$, a sufficiently large fixed multiple of $(1+M_R)W$ is a supersolution on $R_1\le r\le R$. To see this, use $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\le a+b$ and <a href="#q4:var:tail-barrier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:tail-barrier">[q4:var:tail-barrier]</a>; choose the multiple also to dominate $M_R$ on $S_{R_1}$. It dominates the zero outer value. Comparison is valid by writing the difference of the two gradient nonlinearities as a bounded drift. Therefore $$0\le\phi_R\le C(1+M_R)W\qquad (R_1\le r\le R).
\label{q4:var:tail-bound}$$

If $M_R$ diverged along a sequence, normalize by $M_R$. Local mixed estimates near $S$ and interior estimates elsewhere give a subsequential limit $z$ on every fixed compact set. More precisely, <a href="#q4:var:tail-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:tail-bound">[q4:var:tail-bound]</a> bounds $\phi_R/M_R$ on a neighborhood of the fixed closed core. Local Neumann $W^{2,p}$ estimates at $S$, and interior $W^{2,p}$ estimates away from it, give uniform bounds there for $p>4$. Compactness in $C^1$ on the closed core retains both $\sup_{\mathrm{core}}z=1$ and $\partial_\nu z=0$. The limit satisfies $-\Delta_gz=d_0|\,\mathrm dz|_g$, homogeneous Neumann data on $S$, and, by <a href="#q4:var:tail-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:tail-bound">[q4:var:tail-bound]</a>, $z\to0$ at infinity. Its positive global maximum is attained in a compact set. The same strong maximum and boundary point principles again give a contradiction. Thus $M_R$ is bounded, and exhaustion produces a smooth solution of <a href="#q4:var:phi-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:phi-equation">[q4:var:phi-equation]</a> with $\phi=O(r^{-2})$.

<a id="q4:var:rescaled-phi"></a>
Here is the derivative control needed later, using only the stated derivatives of the original data. On a fixed annulus in the $y$ variables put $g_\rho(y)=(g_{ij}(\rho y))$, $U_\rho(y)=\rho^2\phi(\rho y)$, and $a_\rho(y)=\rho d_0(\rho y)$. The exact rescaled equation is $$-\Delta_{g_\rho}U_\rho
 =a_\rho\sqrt{|\,\mathrm dU_\rho|_{g_\rho}^2+|y|^{-6}}
       +\rho^{-\delta}|y|^{-4-\delta}.
\label{q4:var:rescaled-phi}$$ The metric components have uniform $C^{1,1}$ bounds from $g-\delta=O_2$. Consequently both the principal coefficients of this Laplacian and its first-order coefficients have uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds for every fixed $\alpha<1$. No third derivative of $g$ is needed. The chosen radial $d_0$ gives $a_\rho=O(\rho^{-q_0})$ with uniform symbol bounds, independently of derivatives of $K$. First-derivative interpolation in the local $W^{2,p}$ estimates gives a uniform $W^{2,p}$ bound on a smaller annulus. Taking $p>4$ controls $\,\mathrm dU_\rho$ in $C^{0,\alpha}$ for some $\alpha>0$. The positive $|y|^{-6}$ term is bounded away from zero there, so the entire right side of <a href="#q4:var:rescaled-phi" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:rescaled-phi">[q4:var:rescaled-phi]</a> is uniformly $C^{0,\alpha}$. The usual Schauder estimate, including the first-order Laplacian coefficients with these $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds, now gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on a further smaller annulus. Scaling back proves $\phi=O_2(r^{-2})$ without an additional metric or tensor falloff derivative. The equation now yields $$d_0\sqrt{|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g^2+r^{-6}}=O(r^{-4-q_0})=o(w),$$ which proves both the differential inequality and the last limit in <a href="#q4:var:phi-properties" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:phi-properties">[q4:var:phi-properties]</a>. The right side of <a href="#q4:var:phi-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:phi-equation">[q4:var:phi-equation]</a> is integrable. The divergence theorem consequently gives a finite limiting physical sphere flux. Its difference from the Euclidean sphere flux tends to zero, since $g-\delta=O(r^{-q})$ and $\,\mathrm d\phi=O(r^{-3})$.

Finally, differentiating Lemma <a href="#q4:var:conformal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:conformal">86</a> at $f=1+s\phi$ gives $$C'_Q=-2\phi C+6[-\Delta_g\phi+K(\nabla\phi,v)],
 \qquad \theta'_Q=-\phi\theta_++3\partial_\nu\phi.$$ On $\mathcal A$ the first term is zero, and on $S$ we have $\theta_+=0$. This proves <a href="#q4:var:strict-derivatives" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:strict-derivatives">[q4:var:strict-derivatives]</a>. On the full end ball bundle, $C=O(r^{-2-q})$, $\phi C=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)$, and $K(\nabla\phi,v)=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)$. Thus the normalized derivative tends uniformly to six. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-77"></a>
#### Feasible variations and a measure identity

<a id="stmt-q4-var-variation-space"></a>
<div id="q4:var:variation-space" class="definition">

<a id="q4:var:momentum-prototype"></a>
**Definition 88** (Variation space). Let $\mathcal V_0$ be the real vector space generated by all smooth compactly supported pairs $(h,p)$ up to $S$ and the following five pairs, cut off smoothly to the end. The scalar pair is $$h_{ij}=r^{-2}\delta_{ij},\qquad p=0.$$ For each vector $e$ in a fixed basis of $\R^4$, the momentum pair has $h=0$ and is defined by $$p-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p)\delta
 =r^{-3}\bigl(e\otimes\widehat x+\widehat x\otimes e
                  -(e\cdot\widehat x)\delta\bigr),
 \qquad \widehat x=x/r.
\label{q4:var:momentum-prototype}$$ Set $\mathcal V=\R Q+\mathcal V_0$. We write its elements as $H=aQ+H_0$, where $H_0=(h_0,p_0)\in\mathcal V_0$.

</div>

<a id="stmt-q4-var-end-variations"></a>
<div id="q4:var:end-variations" class="lemma">

<a id="q4:var:prototype-constraint-decay"></a>
<a id="q4:var:end-value"></a>
**Lemma 89** (End behavior of the variation space). *The five prototypes have independent charge derivatives. For every fixed $H_0\in\mathcal V_0$, $$C'_{H_0}=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)
\label{q4:var:prototype-constraint-decay}$$ uniformly on the full end ball bundle. The coefficient $a$ in Definition <a href="#q4:var:variation-space" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:variation-space">88</a> is uniquely determined, and $$C'_H/w\longrightarrow6a
\label{q4:var:end-value}$$ uniformly there. All elements of $\mathcal V$ have well-defined charge derivatives.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-end-variations"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-end-variations</summary>

*Proof.* Trace reversal on symmetric tensors in dimension four is invertible. The right side of <a href="#q4:var:momentum-prototype" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:momentum-prototype">[q4:var:momentum-prototype]</a>, written as $$D_{ij}=r^{-4}\bigl(e_i x_j+x_i e_j-(e\cdot x)\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ satisfies $\partial_jD_{ij}=0$ and $D_{ij}\widehat x^j=r^{-3}e_i$. The scalar prototype satisfies the Euclidean linearized scalar constraint because $\Delta_\delta r^{-2}=0$ off the origin. With the ADM normalizations <a href="#q4:intro:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:intro:energy">[q4:intro:energy]</a>–<a href="#q4:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:intro:momentum">[q4:intro:momentum]</a>, the scalar prototype has $E'=1$, $P'=0$, and the momentum prototype for $e$ has $E'=0$, $P'=e/3$. Background corrections to these fluxes vanish by the AF estimates, so the derivatives are independent.

On the end, $h_0=O_2(r^{-2})$ and $p_0=O_1(r^{-3})$. Their Euclidean linearized scalar and momentum constraints vanish. Each remaining linear constraint term has a factor from the decaying background: for example, $(g-\delta)\partial^2h_0$, $\partial g\,\partial h_0$, $\partial^2g\,h_0$, $Kp_0$, or $(g-\delta)\partial p_0$ has order at most $r^{-4-q}$. The variation of the vector identification contributes $-J(h_0^\sharp v)$, of the same order. This proves <a href="#q4:var:prototype-constraint-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:prototype-constraint-decay">[q4:var:prototype-constraint-decay]</a>. Lemma <a href="#q4:var:strict-direction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:strict-direction">87</a> then proves <a href="#q4:var:end-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:end-value">[q4:var:end-value]</a> and the uniqueness of $a$: an element of $\mathcal V_0$ cannot have the normalized end derivative of $Q$.

Compact variations have zero charge derivatives. The prototypes have the fluxes just computed. For $Q$, the momentum derivative is zero and $$E'_Q=-\frac1\omega\lim_{R\to\infty}
              \int_{|x|=R}\partial_r\phi\,\,\mathrm dA_\delta,$$ which is finite by Lemma <a href="#q4:var:strict-direction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:strict-direction">87</a>. Products with background errors have zero limiting flux. Linearity completes the proof. ◻

</details>

Let $\mathcal T$ be the compact space of minimizing frontiers for $g$, with their filled sets, from Proposition <a href="#q4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:area-derivative">84</a>. For $T\in\mathcal T$, write <a id="q4:var:fixed-area-derivative"></a>$$a'_T(h)=\tfrac12\int_T\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T h\,\,\mathrm dA_g.
\label{q4:var:fixed-area-derivative}$$ This is a continuous function of $T$ for each fixed variation $h$.

<a id="stmt-q4-var-feasible-path"></a>
<div id="q4:var:feasible-path" class="lemma">

<a id="q4:var:nonlinear-path"></a>
**Lemma 90** (Strict linear inequalities give feasible nonlinear data). *Suppose $H=aQ+H_0\in\mathcal V$ has $a>0$ and, for some $\varepsilon>0$, $$C'_H\ge\varepsilon w\text{ on }\mathcal A,\qquad
 -\theta'_H>0\text{ on }S.$$ Then, for every sufficiently small $s>0$, $$g_s=e^{2as\phi}(g+sh_0),\qquad
 K_s=e^{as\phi}(K+sp_0)
\label{q4:var:nonlinear-path}$$ satisfies every hypothesis of Theorem <a href="#q4:thm:numerical-provider" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:thm:numerical-provider">80</a>. Its boundary has strictly negative future expansion. The path has derivative $H$, is uniformly comparable to $g$, has uniform large-sphere barriers, and its charges are differentiable at $s=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-feasible-path"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-feasible-path</summary>

*Proof.* Positivity of the metric and uniform comparability hold for small $s$, since $h_0$ and $\phi$ are bounded relative to $g$. They also give completeness with the boundary included. The topology, smoothness, end count and orientability remain those of $\Omega$.

<a id="q4:var:component-remainders"></a>
We check DEC on the whole ball of test vectors. First use the intermediate metric and tensor $\overline g_s=g+sh_0$, $\overline K_s=K+sp_0$, identifying its vector ball with that of $g$ by $\overline I_s$. For sufficiently large $r$, Taylor expansion and the Euclidean cancellations in Lemma <a href="#q4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:end-variations">89</a> give, uniformly in $|v|_g\le1$, $$\overline C_s(x,\overline I_sv)
    =C(x,v)+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}).$$ Here the remainder is uniform in $r$, $s$ in a fixed small interval, and the whole vector ball. To check all its components, the coordinate constraint expressions have the schematic forms $$\begin{aligned}
 R_g&=g^{-1}\partial^2g+\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})(\partial g)^2,\\
 J&=\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})\partial K
       +\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})(\partial g)K,
\end{aligned}$$ and $2\mu-R_g$ is quadratic in $K$, with smooth coefficients in $g^{-1}$. Each second $s$ derivative on the intermediate path is $O(r^{-6})$: the largest terms are $h_0\partial^2h_0$, $(\partial h_0)^2$, $p_0^2$, $h_0\partial p_0$, and $(\partial h_0)p_0$. Terms containing an original $K$, $\partial K$, or background metric derivative decay faster. This calculation includes all occurrences of $\tau=g^{ij}K_{ij}$, without a separate trace estimate. The vector identification also has the uniform matrix expansion $$\overline I_s=(\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}+s h_0^\sharp)^{-1/2}
       =\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-\tfrac{s}{2}h_0^\sharp+O(s^2r^{-4});$$ the eigenvalues lie in a fixed positive interval, so the matrix-function Taylor bound is uniform. Multiplication by the original or varied momentum covector keeps the same remainder order. In fact the preceding calculation gives the componentwise estimates $$\begin{aligned}
 \overline\mu_s&=\mu+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}),\\
 \overline J_s&=J+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}).
\end{aligned}
\label{q4:var:component-remainders}$$

<a id="q4:var:end-feasibility-expansion"></a>
Apply Lemma <a href="#q4:var:conformal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:conformal">86</a> to these intermediate data with $f_s=e^{as\phi}$. After multiplication by the positive factor $f_s^2$, the constraint for the final data is $$C(x,v)+s\bigl(6aw+o(w)\bigr)+O(s^2r^{-6}),
\label{q4:var:end-feasibility-expansion}$$ again uniformly for the full vector ball. Indeed, $-\Delta_g\phi/w\to1$ and $K(\nabla\phi,v)=o(w)$. Changing the metric, tensor, and vector identification in these conformal differential terms adds only the above decay orders, while the extra exponential term uses $|\,\mathrm d\phi|^2=O(r^{-6})$. Since $a>0$ and $r^{-6}=O(w)$, one can first choose a fixed large radius so the coefficient of $s$ in <a href="#q4:var:end-feasibility-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:end-feasibility-expansion">[q4:var:end-feasibility-expansion]</a> is positive, and then choose $s$ small so its remainder is absorbed. DEC follows on this fixed far end, using $C\ge0$.

The remaining base region and its closed unit ball bundle are compact. The derivative of the constraint is strictly positive on its original zero set. By continuity it is positive on a neighborhood of that zero set; on the complement the original constraint has a positive minimum. A uniform Taylor expansion therefore gives $C_s\ge0$ everywhere in the compact region for small positive $s$. The same compactness argument on $S$, where $\theta_+=0$, gives $\theta_{+,s}<0$.

The new densities are integrable componentwise, not merely after contraction with active vectors. The exact conformal formulas give $$\begin{aligned}
 f_sJ_s&=\overline J_s+
            3as\overline K_s(\nabla_{\overline g_s}\phi,\cdot),\\
 f_s^2\mu_s&=\overline\mu_s-3as\Delta_{\overline g_s}\phi
                          -3a^2s^2|\,\mathrm d\phi|_{\overline g_s}^2.
\end{aligned}$$ The extra covector in the first line is $O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6})$. Also $\Delta_{\overline g_s}\phi=\Delta_g\phi+O(sr^{-6})$, with $\Delta_g\phi=O(w)$. Together with <a href="#q4:var:component-remainders" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:component-remainders">[q4:var:component-remainders]</a>, these identities express the new densities as bounded smooth scaling factors times the original integrable densities, plus integrable errors of orders $r^{-4-\delta}$, $r^{-4-q}$, and $r^{-6}$. Uniform metric comparability controls both norms and volume elements. The differentiated falloff has exponent $\min(q,2)>1$, uniformly for $s$ in a small fixed interval, so large coordinate spheres remain mean convex uniformly.

The charge limits can also be checked before differentiation. Write $\pi=K-\tau g$. Since conformal trace reversal gives $\pi_s=f_s(\overline K_s-\overline\tau_s\overline g_s)$, expansion on the end yields $$\pi_s=\pi+s\bigl(p_0-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p_0)\delta\bigr)
          +O(sr^{-3-q})+O(s^2r^{-5}).$$ The terms with the original trace are of size $h_0K=O(r^{-3-q})$; multiplication by $f_s-1=O(sr^{-2})$ adds only the displayed error orders. All errors have zero limiting sphere flux. Therefore $P_s=P+sP'_{H_0}$ in the prescribed coordinates, without an extra decay assumption on $\tau$. Similarly, $$g_s-g-s(h_0+2a\phi g)=O_1(s^2r^{-4}),$$ whose energy flux vanishes. The finite flux of $\phi$ and the scalar prototype thus give $E_s=E+sE'_H$. In particular both charge functions exist and are differentiable with the derivatives computed in Lemma <a href="#q4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:end-variations">89</a>. The path and its first two parameter derivatives are uniformly bounded relative to $g$, as required by Proposition <a href="#q4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:area-derivative">84</a>. This verifies all claims and all hypotheses of the numerical theorem. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-var-multiplier"></a>
<div id="q4:var:multiplier" class="proposition">

<a id="q4:var:measure-identity"></a>
**Proposition 91** (Multiplier identity at equality). *There exist a probability measure $\varpi$ on $\mathcal T$, a nonnegative finite measure $\eta$ on $S$, a nonnegative locally finite measure $\Lambda$ on $\mathcal A$, and $z\ge0$, with $\int_{\mathcal A}w\,\,\mathrm d\Lambda<\infty$, such that for every $H=aQ+H_0=(h,p)\in\mathcal V$, $$6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\int_{\mathcal T}a'_T(h)\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)
   =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
      -\int_S\theta'_H\,\,\mathrm d\eta+za.
\label{q4:var:measure-identity}$$ The constraint pairing is absolutely defined, since $C'_H/w$ is bounded on the compactified active set.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-multiplier"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-multiplier</summary>

<a id="q4:var:separation-map"></a>
*Proof.* Compactify $\mathcal A$ by one end point. If $\mathcal A$ is already compact, adjoin an isolated point; if it is empty, use just that point. The ball fibers are compact and the base has one end, so this is a compact Hausdorff space, denoted $\overline{\mathcal A}$. By Lemma <a href="#q4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:end-variations">89</a>, $C'_H/w$ extends continuously to it with value $6a$ at the added point. On the disjoint compact union $$\mathcal K=\overline{\mathcal A}\sqcup S\sqcup\mathcal T$$ consider the linear map to $C(\mathcal K)$ whose three components are $$H\longmapsto
 \left(\frac{C'_H}{w},\ -\theta'_H,\
                   c a'_T(h)-6\omega\mathcal E'(H)\right).
\label{q4:var:separation-map}$$

Its image does not meet the open cone of functions strictly positive everywhere. Otherwise its value at the added point gives $a>0$, and Lemma <a href="#q4:var:feasible-path" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:feasible-path">90</a> supplies actual feasible data <a href="#q4:var:nonlinear-path" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:nonlinear-path">[q4:var:nonlinear-path]</a>. Let $a(s)$ be their enclosing infimum. The area derivative formula in Proposition <a href="#q4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:area-derivative">84</a> gives $$a'(0+)=\min_{T\in\mathcal T}a'_T(h).$$ Strict positivity of the third component in <a href="#q4:var:separation-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:separation-map">[q4:var:separation-map]</a>, and compactness of $\mathcal T$, imply $$\left.\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}\right|_{0+}
   6\omega\bigl(\mathcal E(g_s,K_s)-\mathfrak m(a(s))\bigr)
   =6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\min_{T\in\mathcal T}a'_T(h)<0.$$ The expression starts at zero and is nonnegative by <a href="#q4:var:nonnegative-defect" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:nonnegative-defect">[q4:var:nonnegative-defect]</a>, a contradiction.

Hahn–Banach separation of a linear subspace from this open convex cone gives a nonzero positive continuous functional on $C(\mathcal K)$ annihilating the image. The subspace need not be closed: its closure is still disjoint from the open cone. The Riesz representation theorem identifies the functional with a nonzero finite positive measure on $\mathcal K$.

Its mass on $\mathcal T$ is positive. If that mass were zero, testing $Q$ would give a strictly positive value on every remaining component: $C'_Q/w\ge6$ on $\mathcal A$, the added-point value is six, and $-\theta'_Q=3$ on $S$. This would contradict annihilation. Normalize the mass on $\mathcal T$ to one and call the resulting measure there $\varpi$. Call its restriction to $S$ $\eta$. On $\mathcal A$, divide the remaining measure by the positive function $w$ to obtain $\Lambda$; this is locally finite and has finite weighted mass. If the normalized added-point mass is $\lambda_\infty$, put $z=6\lambda_\infty$. Rearranging annihilation of <a href="#q4:var:separation-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:separation-map">[q4:var:separation-map]</a> is exactly <a href="#q4:var:measure-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:measure-identity">[q4:var:measure-identity]</a>. ◻

</details>

The separation argument has supplied a probability measure on all minimizing enclosures, not a fixed-horizon first variation. Our next task is to remove its interior support. We do this before extracting a homogeneous adjoint field: compact normal motions test the trace of $K$ on the minimizing frontiers, and the resulting MOTS equation brings outermostness into the argument.

<a id="pm-h-78"></a>
#### Normal graph tests

The measure $\varpi$ may initially be supported on several enclosures of the same area. The next argument uses variations of the original data to show that it is supported on the original horizon. It is local in the open exterior and assumes no complete ambient development.

<a id="stmt-q4-var-normal-tests"></a>
<div id="q4:var:normal-tests" class="lemma">

**Lemma 92** (Compact normal tests annihilating active constraints). *For every $\ell\in C^\infty_c(\operatorname{int}\Omega)$, there are smooth variations $H_j=(h_j,p_j)\in\mathcal V_0$, all supported in one fixed compact subset of the open exterior, such that $$h_j=2\ell K,\qquad C'_{H_j}\longrightarrow0$$ uniformly on the active rays over that compact set.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-normal-tests"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-normal-tests</summary>

*Proof.* Choose a relatively compact open neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\ell$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$ and apply Lemma <a href="#lem:variation:dust-tests" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:variation:dust-tests">14</a> there in spatial dimension four, with $s=\ell$ and $\delta=1/j$. The present densities already satisfy $2\mu=R_g+(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gK)^2-|K|_g^2$ and $J=\operatorname{div}_g(K-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gK)g)$, with $\mu\ge|J|_g$. The smoothness and future-normal convention <a href="#q4:eq:intro-second-fundamental-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:eq:intro-second-fundamental-form">[q4:eq:intro-second-fundamental-form]</a> are precisely those of the lemma. Equation <a href="#q4:var:active-set" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:active-set">[q4:var:active-set]</a> defines the same constraint $C=2(\mu+J(v))$ and the same isometric ray transport, so its derivative is the derivative $\mathfrak C'$ in that lemma.

The resulting pairs have metric component $2\ell K$ and fixed compact support in the open exterior. They therefore belong to $\mathcal V_0$ by Definition <a href="#q4:var:variation-space" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:variation-space">88</a>, and the lemma gives the asserted uniform convergence, including active rays at which $\mu=0$. Their charge, boundary, and end-coefficient variations vanish because the support stays strictly inside the open exterior. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-var-area-localization"></a>
<div id="q4:var:area-localization" class="proposition">

<a id="q4:var:localized-area"></a>
<a id="q4:var:localized-identity"></a>
**Proposition 93** (Localization of the area multiplier). *For $\varpi$-almost every element of $\mathcal T$, its frontier equals $S$, where $\varpi$ is the measure in Proposition <a href="#q4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:multiplier">91</a>. Consequently, for every variation $H=(h,p)$ in $\mathcal V$, $$\int_{\mathcal T}a'_T(h)\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)
       =a'_S(h)=\tfrac12\int_S\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_S h\,\,\mathrm dA_g.
\label{q4:var:localized-area}$$ In particular the multiplier identity becomes $$6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\,a'_S(h)
  =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
       -\int_S\theta'_H\,\,\mathrm d\eta+za.
\label{q4:var:localized-identity}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-var-area-localization"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-var-area-localization</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Equation <a href="#q4:var:measure-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:measure-identity">[q4:var:measure-identity]</a> to the variations in Lemma <a href="#q4:var:normal-tests" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:normal-tests">92</a>. Their charge, boundary, and end-coefficient terms vanish, and $\Lambda$ is finite over their fixed compact support. Since the metric component is $2\ell K$ and $c>0$, uniform convergence of the active constraint derivatives gives <a id="q4:var:trace-test"></a>$$\int_{\mathcal T}\int_T\ell\,\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T K\,\,\mathrm dA_g\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }\ell\in C^\infty_c(\operatorname{int}\Omega).
\label{q4:var:trace-test}$$

Propositions <a href="#q4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:minimizing-hull">83</a> and <a href="#q4:enc:common-plane" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:enc:common-plane">85</a> give exactly the geometry needed for Proposition <a href="#prop:variation:smooth-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:variation:smooth-localization">15</a>: the full frontiers have area $A$, lie in one compact set, have smooth minimal free parts and $C^{1,1}$ contact graphs, and carry a continuous common tangent plane away from $S$. The surface-area kernel is measurable by the tangent-plane measure topology. Their end sides are connected, and each entire smooth frontier is an admissible full cut; no component or contact area is discarded.

Definition <a href="#q4:def:horizon" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:def:horizon">81</a> supplies connectedness and marginality of $S$, outer area-minimality, and the wholly-interior outermostness condition in case <span class="upright">(a)</span> of Proposition <a href="#prop:variation:smooth-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:variation:smooth-localization">15</a>. Hence almost every frontier equals $S$. Its area-derivative conclusion gives Equation <a href="#q4:var:localized-area" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:localized-area">[q4:var:localized-area]</a>; substituting this into Equation <a href="#q4:var:measure-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:measure-identity">[q4:var:measure-identity]</a> gives Equation <a href="#q4:var:localized-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:var:localized-identity">[q4:var:localized-identity]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="q4:adj:section"></a>
### A causal stationary field on the original exterior

We continue with the original equality data $(\Omega,g,K)$ of Definition <a href="#q4:def:horizon" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:def:horizon">81</a>. In particular, $S=\partial\Omega$ is connected, $\theta_+=0$ on $S$, and $S$ is outer area-minimizing. The constants fixed in Section <a href="#q4:var:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:section">16</a> are $$r_0=\sqrt{2m},\qquad b^0=\frac E m,\qquad b^i=-\frac{P_i}{m},
 \qquad c=\frac2{r_0},\qquad \kappa=\frac c2=\frac1{r_0}.$$ Thus $(b^0)^2-|b|^2=1$ and $b^0>0$. We fix the same exponent $1<q_0<\min\{q,2\}$ as in the strict variation constructed there. The purpose of this section is to extract a smooth field from the multiplier and to retain all information about the original second fundamental form.

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-causal-field"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:causal-field" class="theorem">

**Theorem 94** (Causal stationary field). *There are a smooth function $u$ and a smooth vector field $X$ on $\Omega$, smooth up to its one-sided boundary, with the following properties.*

<a id="q4:adj:complementarity"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:kid-first"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:conformal-adjoint"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:kid-second"></a>
1.  *They satisfy $u\ge |X|_g$, $u>0$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$, and $$u\mu+J(X)=0.
     \label{q4:adj:complementarity}$$ With symmetric indices denoting averaging, their equations are $$\begin{aligned}
     \nabla_{(i}X_{j)}&=-uK_{ij},
     \label{q4:adj:kid-first}\\
     \Delta u&=-\operatorname{div}_g\bigl(K(X,\cdot)^\sharp\bigr),
     \label{q4:adj:conformal-adjoint}\\
     \nabla^2u
     &=u(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g+\tau K-2K^2)-\mathcal L_XK+X_{(i}J_{j)}.
     \label{q4:adj:kid-second}
    \end{aligned}$$ Here $X_i=g_{ij}X^j$ and $(K^2)_{ij}=K_{ik}K^k{}_j$.*

<a id="q4:adj:decay"></a>
2.  *On the chosen asymptotically flat end, $$(u,X)=(b^0,b)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).
     \label{q4:adj:decay}$$*

<a id="q4:adj:horizon-data"></a>
3.  *At the boundary, for the unit normal $\nu$ pointing into $\Omega$, $$X=u\nu,\qquad
     \partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)=\kappa.
     \label{q4:adj:horizon-data}$$ Either $u>0$ everywhere on $S$ or $u=0$ everywhere on $S$.*

<a id="q4:adj:stationary-metric"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:ricci"></a>
4.  *On $\mathbb R\times\operatorname{int}\Omega$, set $$\mathbf g=-u^2\,\mathrm dt^2
       +g_{ij}(\mathrm dx^i+X^i\,\mathrm dt)
              (\mathrm dx^j+X^j\,\mathrm dt),
     \qquad \xi=\partial_t,\qquad N=u^2-|X|_g^2.
     \label{q4:adj:stationary-metric}$$ For the future normal $n=u^{-1}(\xi-X)$, the slice $t=0$ has exactly the original induced metric $g$ and second fundamental form $K$, with the convention of Theorem <a href="#q4:thm:rigidity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:thm:rigidity">82</a>. Moreover, $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(\xi,\cdot)=0,
     \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}=0\quad\hbox{on }\{N>0\}.
     \label{q4:adj:ricci}$$*

<a id="q4:adj:positive-collar"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:zero-collar"></a>
5.  *We have $N\ge0$, $N\to1$ at infinity, and $N>0$ in a full collar just outside $S$. More precisely, in the positive boundary-lapse case, $$N|_S=0,\qquad
     \mathrm dN|_S=2u\kappa\,\nu^\flat=2\kappa X^\flat.
     \label{q4:adj:positive-collar}$$ In the zero boundary-lapse case, if $s\ge0$ is the original $g$-normal distance from $S$, there are smooth one-sided fields $d,Y_2$ such that $$u=sd,\qquad X=s^2Y_2,\qquad d|_S=\kappa,\qquad
     N=s^2\bigl(d^2-s^2|Y_2|_g^2\bigr).
     \label{q4:adj:zero-collar}$$ Consequently all zeros of $N$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$ lie in a compact subset of that interior.*

</div>

The proof occupies the remainder of this section. At no point do we assume that the original data are vacuum or that they lie in a prescribed stationary development. The metric in <a href="#q4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:stationary-metric">[q4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> is constructed from the multiplier.

<a id="q4:adj:measures"></a>
#### From a positive measure to the interior adjoint equations

<a id="q4:adj:localized-multiplier"></a>
By Proposition <a href="#q4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:multiplier">91</a> and the area localization in Proposition <a href="#q4:var:area-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:area-localization">93</a>, the multiplier identity is $$6\omega\,\mathcal E'(H)-c\,a'_S(h)
 =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
   -\int_S\theta'_H\,\mathrm d\eta+za,
 \qquad H=aQ+H_0.
 \label{q4:adj:localized-multiplier}$$ The coefficient $a$ is the coefficient of the strict direction $Q$ in the variation space. We recall that $$C(x,v)=R_g+\tau^2-|K|^2+2J(v),\qquad |v|_g\le1,$$ that $\Lambda$ is a positive locally finite measure on the active set $C=0$, and that the test-vector identification for a metric variation $h$ has $\dot v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v$.

Let $u$ be the scalar pushforward of $\Lambda$ to $\Omega$, and let $X$ be its vector first moment. Initially these symbols denote measures: for a compactly supported scalar $f$ and covector $\alpha$, $$\langle u,f\rangle=\int f(x)\,\mathrm d\Lambda(x,v),
 \qquad
 \langle X,\alpha\rangle=\int\alpha_x(v)\,\mathrm d\Lambda(x,v).$$ The unit-ball condition and positivity give $|X|_g\le u$ as measures, while activity gives $\mu u+J(X)=0$ as a measure. We use $\mathrm dV_g$ as the reference density when expressing the resulting distributional equations. After establishing smoothness, we use the same letters for the smooth densities of these measures.

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-interior-equations"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:interior-equations" class="lemma">

**Lemma 95** (Interior adjoint equations). *The moment measures have smooth densities on $\operatorname{int}\Omega$. They satisfy <a href="#q4:adj:complementarity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:complementarity">[q4:adj:complementarity]</a>–<a href="#q4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-second">[q4:adj:kid-second]</a> there, and $u\ge|X|_g$ there.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-interior-equations"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-interior-equations</summary>

*Proof.* For a variation supported in the open exterior, every term of <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> except the constraint pairing vanishes. For a pure tensor variation $p=\dot K$, that pairing is $$2\bigl\langle u,\tau\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g p-K:p\bigr\rangle
 +2\bigl\langle X,\nabla^j(p_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g p)g_{ij})\bigr\rangle.$$ Its distributional adjoint equation is <a id="q4:adj:tensor-adjoint"></a>$$u(\tau g-K)-\nabla_{(i}X_{j)}+(\operatorname{div}X)g=0.
 \label{q4:adj:tensor-adjoint}$$ Taking the trace in four dimensions gives $3u\tau+3\operatorname{div}X=0$. Substitution proves <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a>.

For the conformal variation $(h,p)=(2\psi g,\psi K)$, the constraint transformation already established in Section <a href="#q4:var:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:section">16</a> gives, on active rays, $$C'_H(x,v)=6\{-\Delta\psi+K(\nabla\psi,v)\}.$$ Its adjoint is <a href="#q4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[q4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a>. This calculation is valid for measure moments, so both equations hold in distributions before any regularity assertion.

Diverge <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a> and substitute $\operatorname{div}X=-u\tau$. Commuting covariant derivatives gives a Laplace equation for $X$ whose right side consists of smooth coefficients times $u,X,\nabla u$. In <a href="#q4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[q4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a>, the right side consists of smooth coefficients times $X,\nabla X$. Thus the coupled system has diagonal Laplace principal part on the scalar and vector bundles; all couplings have order at most one. Distributional interior elliptic regularity, iterated with the smooth coefficients, makes both densities smooth. The measure inequalities and complementarity now give the asserted pointwise statements.

<a id="q4:adj:metric-functional"></a>
It remains to verify the full metric equation, including its matter term. We may now work with smooth $u,X$. For a pure metric variation $h$, keep covariant $K$, scalar $u$, and contravariant $X$ fixed. The constraint pairing is the variation of $$\int\bigl[u(R+\tau^2-|K|^2)
      +2X^i\nabla^j(K_{ij}-\tau g_{ij})\bigr]\,\mathrm dV_g
 \label{q4:adj:metric-functional}$$ minus $\int h(X,J^\sharp)\,\mathrm dV_g$. The latter is precisely the contribution of $\dot v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v$. In using the varying volume form in <a href="#q4:adj:metric-functional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:metric-functional">[q4:adj:metric-functional]</a>, no term has been added: its original integrand is $2u\mu+2J(X)=0$ pointwise.

<a id="q4:adj:shift-coefficient"></a>
For completeness, put $\pi^{ij}=K^{ij}-\tau g^{ij}$. Integrating the shift term once by parts gives $-\int\pi^{ij}(\mathcal L_Xg)_{ij}\,\mathrm dV_g$, with unchanged boundary terms outside the variation support. At fixed covariant $K$, $$\delta\pi^{ij}
 =-h^i{}_aK^{aj}-h^j{}_aK^{ia}
   +(K:h)g^{ij}+\tau h^{ij}.$$ Variation of the last integral, followed by integration of the term $-\pi^{ij}(\mathcal L_Xh)_{ij}$, has coefficient $$\mathcal L_XK-(\operatorname{div}X)K
  -\{X(\tau)+K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b\}g.
 \label{q4:adj:shift-coefficient}$$ One can see the cancellations directly: if $B=\mathcal L_Xg$, the variation of $\pi$ contributes $2\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(KB)-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}B)K-\tau B$; integration of $\mathcal L_Xh$ contributes $(\mathcal L_X\pi)^{ij}+(\operatorname{div}X)\pi^{ij}$ with indices lowered; and the volume variation contributes $-\tfrac12(\pi:B)g$. Together they are <a href="#q4:adj:shift-coefficient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:shift-coefficient">[q4:adj:shift-coefficient]</a>.

<a id="q4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:trace-identity"></a>
The scalar and quadratic terms in <a href="#q4:adj:metric-functional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:metric-functional">[q4:adj:metric-functional]</a> have coefficient $$\nabla^2u-(\Delta u)g-u\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g
       +2u(K^2-\tau K)+u\mu g.$$ Adding <a href="#q4:adj:shift-coefficient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:shift-coefficient">[q4:adj:shift-coefficient]</a> and the test-vector correction therefore gives $$\begin{aligned}
 0={}&\nabla^2u-(\Delta u)g-u\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g+2u(K^2-\tau K)+u\mu g
       \notag\\
    &+\mathcal L_XK-(\operatorname{div}X)K
      -\{X(\tau)+K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b\}g-X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{q4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded}
\end{aligned}$$ Equation <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a> gives $K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b=-u|K|^2$. Moreover, using $\nabla^jK_{ij}=J_i+\nabla_i\tau$ in <a href="#q4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[q4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a> gives $$\Delta u+X(\tau)
   =u|K|^2-J(X)=u(|K|^2+\mu).
 \label{q4:adj:trace-identity}$$ Together with $\operatorname{div}X=-u\tau$, these identities cancel the scalar multiples of $g$ in <a href="#q4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded">[q4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded]</a> and give <a href="#q4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-second">[q4:adj:kid-second]</a>. ◻

</details>

The multiplier now has smooth interior densities and satisfies the full adjoint system, including its matter term. To use it as a geometric field we still need its boundary behavior and its normalization at infinity. Both follow from the same equations and the allowed variations; neither is imposed as an additional boundary condition.

<a id="pm-h-81"></a>
#### Boundary regularity and the asymptotic constants

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-boundary-regularity"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:boundary-regularity" class="lemma">

**Lemma 96** (Prolongation and absence of boundary atoms). *The fields $u,X$ extend smoothly to the one-sided boundary $S$. Their first jet at one interior point determines them on the connected interior. The original moment measures have no boundary-supported part, and hence are exactly $u\,\mathrm dV_g$ and $X\,\mathrm dV_g$ on all of $\Omega$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-boundary-regularity"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-boundary-regularity</summary>

<a id="q4:adj:prolongation-x"></a>
<a id="q4:adj:prolongation-u"></a>
*Proof.* Put $B_{ij}=-uK_{ij}$. Differentiate $\nabla_{(i}X_{j)}=B_{ij}$ in three arrangements, add two of the resulting equations, and subtract the third. Commuting derivatives gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_i\nabla_jX_k
 &=\nabla_iB_{jk}+\nabla_jB_{ik}-\nabla_kB_{ij}
       +\mathcal R_{ijk}(X),\label{q4:adj:prolongation-x}\\
 \mathcal R_{ijk}(X)
 &=-\tfrac12\bigl(
       ([\nabla_j,\nabla_i]X)_k
       +([\nabla_i,\nabla_k]X)_j
       +([\nabla_j,\nabla_k]X)_i\bigr).\notag
\end{aligned}$$ Every commutator is a curvature contraction with $X$. Thus this equation uses only $K\nabla u$, $u\nabla K$, and curvature times $X$. Expanding the Lie derivative in <a href="#q4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-second">[q4:adj:kid-second]</a> gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_i\nabla_ju
 ={}&u(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij})-X^a\nabla_aK_{ij}
       \notag\\
 &-K_{aj}\nabla_iX^a-K_{ia}\nabla_jX^a+X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{q4:adj:prolongation-u}
\end{aligned}$$ Consequently $$\mathcal J=(u,X,\nabla u,\nabla X)$$ obeys a homogeneous linear first-order system, with smooth coefficients built from $g,K$, their required derivatives, and $J$. Along any smooth curve, this is a linear ODE for $\mathcal J$. Uniqueness along curves proves the first-jet assertion.

In a compact collar of $S$, start on an interior collar section and solve this ODE along the normal segments down to $S$. Its coefficients are smooth up to the one-sided boundary. Smooth dependence on the initial point and on the normal parameter provides the smooth extension, agreeing with the original solution for positive collar parameter. The pointwise inequalities and complementarity extend by continuity.

The original moments could still have parts supported on $S$; the interior regularity alone does not exclude them. Let $s$ be geodesic collar distance, let $f\in C^\infty(S)$ be arbitrary and extended constantly along the normal segments, and take a collar cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $S$. Choose the compact pure metric variation <a id="q4:adj:boundary-atom-test"></a>$$h=\frac{s^2\chi(s)f}{6}\bigl(g-\mathrm ds\otimes\mathrm ds\bigr),
 \qquad p=0.
 \label{q4:adj:boundary-atom-test}$$ This is one of the allowed smooth compact variations, with strict-direction coefficient $a=0$. Its value and first jet vanish on $S$. The trace along the three-dimensional collar slices is $s^2\chi f/2$, so its second normal derivative at $S$ is $f$. At $S$, the scalar variation $$R'_g(h)=\nabla^i\nabla^jh_{ij}-\Delta(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gh)-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g:h$$ therefore equals $-f$: the only nonzero second jets are normal-normal derivatives of tangential components, whereas $h_{ss}=h_{sA}=0$. The variation of $\tau^2-|K|^2$ uses only $h$, that of $J$ at fixed covariant $K$ uses only $h,\nabla h$, and the test-vector correction uses only $h$. Consequently $C'_H|_S=-f$, independently of the active ray $v$.

The area derivative vanishes because $h|_S=0$; the expansion derivative vanishes because $h|_S=\nabla h|_S=p|_S=0$; and the charge derivative vanishes by compact support. Integrating the smooth interior densities by parts gives zero as well: the adjoint vanishes, and its scalar boundary terms involve only $h,\nabla h$, while its momentum boundary terms involve only $h$. This is ordinary integration up to $S$ using the one-sided smooth fields, not distributional differentiation of a zero extension across $S$. Thus <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> says that the scalar boundary measure annihilates every $f\in C^\infty(S)$, and that measure is zero. The inequality $|X|_g\le u$ as measures eliminates the vector boundary part. Moreover, since $u$ is the pushforward of the positive measure $\Lambda$, the entire measure $\Lambda$ has zero mass over $S$, not merely zero first moment there. ◻

</details>

We first obtain constant limits from a Hessian estimate and causality. Related radial estimates for asymptotic Killing fields appear in (Beig and Chruściel 1996, Proposition 2.1 and Appendix C) <a id="pm-cite-78"></a>[[BeigChrusciel1996](#ref-BeigChrusciel1996)]. The normalization of the limits will then follow from the end variations.

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics" class="lemma">

<a id="q4:adj:jet-estimate"></a>
**Lemma 97** (Asymptotics of causal fields). *Let $g$ be a smooth metric uniformly comparable to the Euclidean metric on an end $\R^4\setminus\overline B_R$. Let $u$ be a smooth function and $X$ a smooth vector field there with $u\ge |X|_g$. Write $Y$ for all coordinate components of $(u,X)$. Suppose that, for some $q_0>1$ and a constant $C$, the coordinate derivatives satisfy $$|\partial^2Y|
 \le C r^{-1-q_0}|\partial Y|+C r^{-2-q_0}|Y|.
 \label{q4:adj:jet-estimate}$$ Then there are constants $u_\infty$ and $X_\infty\in\R^4$ such that $$(u,X)=(u_\infty,X_\infty)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics</summary>

*Proof.* Fix a sufficiently large coordinate sphere of radius $R$ and put $$D(r)=\sup_{\omega\in S^3}|\partial Y(r\omega)|,
 \qquad \mathcal M(r)=\sup_{R\le t\le r}D(t).$$ Along each ray, $|Y(t\omega)|\le C+\int_R^tD(a)\,\mathrm da\le C+t\mathcal M(t)$, uniformly in $\omega$. Integrating $\partial_r(\partial Y)$ using <a href="#q4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:jet-estimate">[q4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>, and then taking the supremum over directions and radii at most $r$, gives $$\mathcal M(r)\le C+C\int_R^r t^{-1-q_0}\mathcal M(t)\,\mathrm dt.$$ The kernel is integrable. Gronwall therefore bounds $\mathcal M$ uniformly, so $\partial Y=O(1)$ and $Y=O(r)$. Equation <a href="#q4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:jet-estimate">[q4:adj:jet-estimate]</a> now gives $\partial^2Y=O(r^{-1-q_0})$. Each coordinate derivative has a radial limit $L(\omega)$, with error $O(r^{-q_0})$. Any two points on the sphere of radius $r$ can be joined by a spherical arc of length at most $\pi r$; integrating the Hessian along this arc gives an $O(r^{-q_0})$ difference between their gradients. Letting $r\to\infty$ shows that $L(\omega)$ is one constant matrix $L$. Radial integration of $\partial Y-L$ then gives $$\partial Y=L+O(r^{-q_0}),\qquad Y=Lx+O(1),$$ where boundedness of the second error uses $q_0>1$. Since $u\ge0$ in every direction, the linear part of $u$ vanishes. Uniform comparability of $g$ with the Euclidean metric and $|X|_g\le u$ then force the linear part of $X$ to vanish as well. Thus $Y=O(1)$ and $\partial Y=O(r^{-q_0})$. Substitution in <a href="#q4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:jet-estimate">[q4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>, using $q_0>1$, improves the Hessian bound to $O(r^{-2-q_0})$. Integrating each gradient component radially toward its zero limit gives $\partial Y=O(r^{-1-q_0})$. A further radial integration gives $Y=B(\omega)+O(r^{-q_0})$; comparison of values along the same spherical arcs now gives an $O(r^{-q_0})$ difference, so $B$ too is independent of direction. This proves the asserted constant limit and both differentiated estimates. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-asymptotics"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:asymptotics" class="lemma">

**Lemma 98** (Asymptotic normalization and positive lapse). *Equation <a href="#q4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:decay">[q4:adj:decay]</a> holds, and $u>0$ on $\operatorname{int}\Omega$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-asymptotics"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-asymptotics</summary>

*Proof.* Let $Y$ denote all coordinate components of the pair $(u,X)$. The prolonged system and the original $O_2$ metric and $O_1$ tensor decay imply Equation <a href="#q4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:jet-estimate">[q4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>. Indeed curvature, $\nabla K$, and $J$ have order $-2-q_0$, while $K$ and the Christoffel symbols have order $-1-q_0$. Equations <a href="#q4:adj:prolongation-x" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:prolongation-x">[q4:adj:prolongation-x]</a> and <a href="#q4:adj:prolongation-u" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:prolongation-u">[q4:adj:prolongation-u]</a> use no higher background derivatives. Converting their covariant Hessians to coordinate Hessians adds terms with coefficients $\Gamma$, $\partial\Gamma$, and $\Gamma^2$, controlled by the stated $O_2$ metric decay.

<a id="q4:adj:unnormalized-decay"></a>
Lemma <a href="#q4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics">97</a> now gives constants with $$(u,X)=(u_\infty,X_\infty)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).
 \label{q4:adj:unnormalized-decay}$$

<a id="q4:adj:charge-flux"></a>
Use the five end prototypes of Definition <a href="#q4:var:variation-space" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:variation-space">88</a>, whose charge derivatives are computed in Lemma <a href="#q4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:var:end-variations">89</a>, in <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a>. Their strict-direction coefficient is $a=0$, so the term $za$ is absent; their boundary and area terms vanish because the prototypes are supported away from $S$. Integration by parts using the interior adjoint equations leaves only the outer boundary flux. By <a href="#q4:adj:unnormalized-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:unnormalized-decay">[q4:adj:unnormalized-decay]</a>, its limit is $$6\omega\bigl(u_\infty E'+X_\infty^iP'_i\bigr).
 \label{q4:adj:charge-flux}$$ For clarity, the leading integrand is $$u_\infty(\partial_jh_{ij}-\partial_i h_{jj})
 +2X_\infty^j\bigl(p_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p)\delta_{ij}\bigr).$$ This is exactly <a href="#q4:adj:charge-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:charge-flux">[q4:adj:charge-flux]</a> with the energy and momentum normalizations of Equations <a href="#q4:intro:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:intro:energy">[q4:intro:energy]</a>–<a href="#q4:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:intro:momentum">[q4:intro:momentum]</a>. Every other boundary term contains a decaying background or adjoint coefficient, or its derivative, paired with $h=O_2(r^{-2})$ or $p=O_1(r^{-3})$ at the corresponding order. Multiplication by the sphere area $O(r^3)$ makes each such flux tend to zero. The volume pairing converges as well: the prototype constraint derivatives are $O(r^{-4-q})$ and the moment densities are bounded.

The scalar prototype $h=r^{-2}\delta$, $p=0$, has $(E',P')=(1,0)$. For the tensor prototype indexed by a constant vector $e$, its Euclidean trace reversal contracts with the sphere normal to $r^{-3}e$, and thus has $(E',P')=(0,e/3)$. These independent charges identify $(u_\infty,X_\infty)=(b^0,b)$ from <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> and <a href="#q4:adj:charge-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:charge-flux">[q4:adj:charge-flux]</a>. This proves <a href="#q4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:decay">[q4:adj:decay]</a>.

If $u$ vanished at an interior point, its nonnegativity would give $\mathrm du=0$ there. Taylor’s theorem and $|X|\le u$ would give $X=0$ and $\nabla X=0$ at the same point. The whole first jet would vanish, contradicting Lemma <a href="#q4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:boundary-regularity">96</a> and $u_\infty=b^0>0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-82"></a>
#### Boundary fluxes and the two lapse cases

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-boundary-data"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:boundary-data" class="lemma">

**Lemma 99** (Boundary equations). *The multiplier measure at $S$ is $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$, and <a href="#q4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:horizon-data">[q4:adj:horizon-data]</a> holds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-boundary-data"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-boundary-data</summary>

*Proof.* Take arbitrary compact pure tensor variations up to $S$. The actual outward normal of the exterior domain at its inner boundary is $-\nu$. Integration by parts in <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> therefore gives $$-2\int_S\bigl[p(X,\nu)-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gp)X_\nu\bigr]\,\mathrm dA_g
      -\int_S(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_Sp)\,\mathrm d\eta=0.$$ Arbitrary mixed components $p_{\nu A}$ imply $X_{TS}=0$, and arbitrary tangential trace implies $\mathrm d\eta=2X_\nu\,\mathrm dA_g$.

Now take $(h,p)=(2\psi g,\psi K)$ with arbitrary compact support up to $S$. At a MOTS, its expansion derivative is $3\partial_\nu\psi$, while its area derivative is $3\int_S\psi\,\mathrm dA_g$. Integrating its constraint pairing with <a href="#q4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[q4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a> gives $$\begin{aligned}
 -3c\int_S\psi\,\mathrm dA_g
 ={}&6\int_S\left[u\partial_\nu\psi
       -\{\partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)\}\psi\right]\,\mathrm dA_g
       -3\int_S\partial_\nu\psi\,\mathrm d\eta.
\end{aligned}$$ The boundary value and normal derivative of $\psi$ can be prescribed independently. Their coefficients give $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$ and $\partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)=c/2$. Together with the tensor-variation conclusions these are exactly <a href="#q4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:horizon-data">[q4:adj:horizon-data]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-lapse-dichotomy"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:lapse-dichotomy" class="lemma">

**Lemma 100** (Boundary lapse dichotomy). *Either $u>0$ at every point of $S$ or $u=0$ identically on $S$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-lapse-dichotomy"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-lapse-dichotomy</summary>

*Proof.* Let $L_S$ be the expansion variation at $S$ under normal motion with speed $s\nu$. Its principal part is $-\Delta_S$. More explicitly, in a geodesic normal extension of $\nu$, if $\mathrm{II}$ is the second fundamental form of $S$ in $(\Omega,g)$, $$L_Ss=-\Delta_Ss+2K(\nu,\nabla_Ss)
  +\left[-|\mathrm{II}|^2-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g(\nu,\nu)
          +\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{TS}(\nabla_\nu K)\right]s.$$ Only the smoothness of the lower coefficients and the displayed principal part will be needed.

Extend $s\nu$ to a smooth compactly supported vector field $Y_1$ up to the boundary, and use $H=(\mathcal L_{Y_1}g,\mathcal L_{Y_1}K)$ in <a href="#q4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:localized-multiplier">[q4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a>. These are legitimate one-sided tensor variations; one may compute their jets using any smooth extension across $S$. Their area and expansion derivatives are respectively $\int_SHs\,\mathrm dA_g$ and $L_Ss$.

We check the active-ray derivative with the specified vector identification. At a fixed interior point put $\mathcal A(v)=\nabla_vY_1$, so $h^\sharp=\mathcal A+\mathcal A^*$, where the adjoint uses $g$. Let $\phi_t$ be the local flow of $Y_1$ and let $v_t$ be the isometrically identified test vector for $g_t=\phi_t^*g$. Naturality gives $$C_{\phi_t^*g,\phi_t^*K}(x,v_t)
   =C_{g,K}(\phi_t x,\mathrm d\phi_t(v_t)).$$ At $t=0$, the covariant velocity of the vector on the right, relative to parallel transport along $\phi_t x$, is $$\mathcal A(v)+\dot v
 =\mathcal A(v)-\tfrac12(\mathcal A+\mathcal A^*)v
 =\tfrac12(\mathcal A-\mathcal A^*)v.$$ It is perpendicular to $v$. The base derivative of $C$, with $v$ parallel transported, vanishes at an interior active ray because it differentiates a nonnegative function at a two-sided interior minimum. The remaining vector derivative is $2J(\tfrac12(\mathcal A-\mathcal A^*)v)$, also zero: at an active unit ray $J=-\mu v^\flat$, and at an active ray with $|v|<1$ we have $\mu=J=0$. Therefore $C'_H=0$ at every interior active ray.

The vector field $Y_1$ need not preserve $S$: its compact Lie derivatives are permitted tensor variations, independently of feasibility of a flow on the whole exterior. No normal derivative at a one-sided boundary minimum is being set equal to zero. Such boundary rays contribute no integral because $\Lambda$ has zero mass over $S$ by Lemma <a href="#q4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:boundary-regularity">96</a>. Thus the entire constraint pairing vanishes. The multiplier identity and $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$ now read $$-c\int_S Hs\,\mathrm dA_g=-2\int_SuL_Ss\,\mathrm dA_g,$$ and hence give <a id="q4:adj:boundary-stability-adjoint"></a>$$2L_S^*u=cH.
 \label{q4:adj:boundary-stability-adjoint}$$ Here the adjoint is with respect to $\mathrm dA_g$ on the closed manifold $S$.

Outer area minimization, tested against every nonnegative outward normal speed, gives $H\ge0$ pointwise. Hence $L_S^*u\ge0$ and $u\ge0$ on $S$. Increase the zeroth coefficient of $L_S^*$ by a constant until that coefficient is nonnegative. The inequality remains valid because $u\ge0$. The strong minimum principle for this operator with principal part $-\Delta_S$ shows that a zero of $u$ forces $u$ to vanish on the connected surface $S$. Otherwise it is everywhere positive. ◻

</details>

We have identified the field at the horizon and at infinity. These identities let us construct a stationary spacetime containing the original slice. Causality and complementarity will make that spacetime vacuum on the timelike region; an initially possible null stress must remain in the calculation until that region is identified.

<a id="pm-h-83"></a>
#### The constructed spacetime and its null stress

<a id="stmt-q4-adj-killing-development"></a>
<div id="q4:adj:killing-development" class="lemma">

**Lemma 101** (Killing development and timelike collars). *The metric in <a href="#q4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:stationary-metric">[q4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> has all the properties in parts <span class="upright">(iv)</span> and <span class="upright">(v)</span> of Theorem <a href="#q4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:causal-field">94</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-killing-development"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-killing-development</summary>

*Proof.* The interior positivity of $u$ makes <a href="#q4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:stationary-metric">[q4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> a smooth Lorentzian metric, with future normal $n=u^{-1}(\partial_t-X)$ after choosing the indicated time orientation. In the convention of the problem, the second fundamental form of a lapse-shift metric is $$\frac1{2u}\bigl(\partial_tg-\mathcal L_Xg\bigr).$$ Its coefficients here are independent of $t$, and <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a> identifies this tensor with the original $K$. The vector field $\xi=\partial_t$ is Killing by construction.

<a id="q4:adj:einstein-components"></a>
We record the curvature computation to fix both the matter term and the sign convention. The Gauss and normal-variation identities for a general lapse-shift metric, with positive second fundamental form convention, are $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g,ij}
  &=\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij}
    +u^{-1}\bigl(\partial_tK_{ij}
           -(\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}-(\nabla^2u)_{ij}\bigr),\\
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(n,n)
  &=-u^{-1}(\partial_t\tau-X\tau)-|K|^2+u^{-1}\Delta u.
\end{aligned}$$ Tracing these equations uses $$g^{ij}\bigl(\partial_tK_{ij}-(\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}\bigr)
 =\partial_t\tau-X\tau+2u|K|^2.$$ In the stationary case this yields <a id="q4:adj:spatial-ricci"></a><a id="q4:adj:spacetime-scalar"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g,ij}
 &=\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij}
      -u^{-1}\bigl((\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}+(\nabla^2u)_{ij}\bigr),
 \label{q4:adj:spatial-ricci}\\
 R_{\mathbf g}
 &=R_g+\tau^2+|K|^2-2u^{-1}(\Delta u+X\tau).
 \label{q4:adj:spacetime-scalar}
\end{aligned}$$ Equation <a href="#q4:adj:trace-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:trace-identity">[q4:adj:trace-identity]</a> and complementarity show that $$R_{\mathbf g}=2\mu+\frac{2J(X)}u=0.$$ Writing $\mathbf G$ for the Einstein tensor, the constraints and <a href="#q4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-second">[q4:adj:kid-second]</a> consequently give $$\mathbf G(n,n)=\mu,\qquad
 \mathbf G(n,e_i)=J_i,\qquad
 u\mathbf G_{ij}=-X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{q4:adj:einstein-components}$$ These identities can also be compared with the transversal Killing construction in (Beig and Chruściel 1997) <a id="pm-cite-79"></a>[[BeigChrusciel1997KID](#ref-BeigChrusciel1997KID)]; its momentum symbol has the opposite sign to the one used here. The null-fluid structure of a modified constraint adjoint is discussed in (Huang and Lee 2024, sec. 6.1) <a id="pm-cite-80"></a>[[HuangLee2024Bartnik](#ref-HuangLee2024Bartnik)]. We use the displayed direct calculation, in four spatial dimensions, rather than importing a stationarity or dimensional-transfer theorem.

If $\mu=0$, the dominant energy condition gives $J=0$, so all entries in <a href="#q4:adj:einstein-components" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:einstein-components">[q4:adj:einstein-components]</a> vanish. If $\mu>0$, the inequalities $$0=u\mu+J(X)\ge u\mu-|J||X|\ge0$$ force $|J|=\mu$, $|X|=u$, and $J=-\mu X^\flat/u$. Since $\mathbf g(\xi,n)=-u$ and $\mathbf g(\xi,e_i)=X_i$, the tensor with components <a href="#q4:adj:einstein-components" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:einstein-components">[q4:adj:einstein-components]</a> is exactly <a id="q4:adj:null-stress"></a>$$\mathbf G=\frac\mu{u^2}\,\xi^\flat\otimes\xi^\flat
 \quad\hbox{where }\mu>0.
 \label{q4:adj:null-stress}$$ The Killing one-form in this equation is the spacetime one-form. It is null wherever the displayed tensor is nonzero. Thus $\mathbf G(\xi,\cdot)=0$ everywhere. Since $R_{\mathbf g}=0$, this is the first assertion of <a href="#q4:adj:ricci" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:ricci">[q4:adj:ricci]</a>. If $N>0$, then $|X|<u$, so complementarity forces $\mu=J=0$; all the Ricci components vanish. This proves the second assertion. An internal null region has not been excluded or assumed vacuum.

It remains to examine the original boundary and the end. Equation <a href="#q4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:decay">[q4:adj:decay]</a> gives $N\to(b^0)^2-|b|^2=1$. At $S$, Equation <a href="#q4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:horizon-data">[q4:adj:horizon-data]</a> gives $X=u\nu$, so $N=0$ and all tangential derivatives of $N$ vanish. If $u>0$ on $S$, Equation <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a> gives $\langle\nabla_\nu X,\nu\rangle=-uK(\nu,\nu)$. Hence $$\partial_\nu N
 =2u\bigl(\partial_\nu u+uK(\nu,\nu)\bigr)=2u\kappa,$$ which is <a href="#q4:adj:positive-collar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:positive-collar">[q4:adj:positive-collar]</a>. Compactness of $S$ supplies a full collar on which $N>0$.

In the other case, $u|_S=0$ and $X|_S=0$. Tangential derivatives of $X$ vanish. The normal-normal and normal-tangential components of <a href="#q4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:kid-first">[q4:adj:kid-first]</a> then give $\nabla_\nu X=0$ on $S$, so every first derivative of $X$ vanishes there. Smooth one-sided division by normal distance gives $u=sd$ and $X=s^2Y_2$. The boundary condition gives $d|_S=\partial_\nu u|_S=\kappa>0$. This is <a href="#q4:adj:zero-collar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4:adj:zero-collar">[q4:adj:zero-collar]</a>, and once again compactness gives a full collar with $N>0$. Together with positivity far out on the unique end, these collars place all interior zeros of $N$ in an interior compact set. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4-adj-killing-development-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4-adj-killing-development</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#q4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:causal-field">94</a>.* Combine Lemmas <a href="#q4:adj:interior-equations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:interior-equations">95</a>, <a href="#q4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:boundary-regularity">96</a>, <a href="#q4:adj:asymptotics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:asymptotics">98</a>, <a href="#q4:adj:boundary-data" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:boundary-data">99</a>, <a href="#q4:adj:lapse-dichotomy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:lapse-dichotomy">100</a>, and <a href="#q4:adj:killing-development" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:killing-development">101</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="q4:sta:section"></a>
### The complete static base under weak decay

The causal field of Theorem <a href="#q4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4:adj:causal-field">94</a> satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition <a href="#prop:static:common-base" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:static:common-base">34</a>. We verify that application at the stated weak decay, and record the boundary coordinates needed to recover the original hypersurface.
